description: We are Spectra, building a wearable gadget with multispectral sensors to monitor astronaut health. Our idea combines onboard microcontrollers, machine learning and a dashboard to detect unusual patterns and relay alerts to Earth. Interested in space, health, or hands-on innovation? Join us! We're looking for teammates with skills in embedded systems, sensors, ML, software development, UI/UX, biomedical science and storytelling
summary:
Twenty minutes. That is how long a message from Mars can take to reach Earth, one way. If an astronaut's body starts to change in that gap, mission control cannot help in time.

Spectra moves the first answer on board. A screenless wristband reads pulse, skin temperature, motion and multispectral light. A Raspberry Pi server inside the spacecraft runs machine learning locally: it rejects unreliable readings, compares each one with that astronaut's own pattern, and raises an event only when a change persists. Events are stored on board and reach the ground team when the link allows.

This is running software, not only a concept. Our browser simulator shows the astronaut's view and the ground team's view side by side, including link loss and delay. On 300 held-out sessions, our neural network caught almost eight times more subtle recoveries than a statistical baseline, with zero false alerts. All data is synthetic, and we say so everywhere.

The astronaut gets an answer first. Earth gets the record.
details:
THE PROBLEM

On a Mars mission, a message can take up to 20 minutes to reach Earth, and the link is not always there. NASA expects deep-space crews to solve problems as a team, without immediate help from the ground. Health monitoring that depends on mission control stops working exactly when the crew is most alone.

OUR SOLUTION

Spectra is a health monitoring system that gives the astronaut the first answer on board and gives Earth the full record when communication allows. It has three parts.

1. A screenless wristband (design proposal). A continuous titanium band with a soft inner liner and one sensor module against the skin: multispectral optical sensor, PPG sensor, skin-temperature sensor and accelerometer. Nothing to operate, no extra screen in the astronaut's day.

2. An onboard server (design proposal). A Raspberry Pi in a compact aluminum enclosure. It receives the readings over a local wireless link, runs the analysis, stores events, and hands them to the spacecraft's communication system.

3. The intelligence and the mission simulator (running today). The full pipeline, from a single reading to the ground team's screen, runs in any browser.

HOW IT WORKS

Each window of readings must pass three questions, in order.

- Can this reading be trusted? Lost skin contact, missing data and motion are detected first. An unreliable window is never scored.

- Is it different for this person? A neural network predicts this astronaut's heart rate and skin temperature for the current moment of the activity, learned from their own reference sessions rather than a population average.

- Does the change persist? One odd reading is not an alert. Spectra asks for a check only after three consecutive windows above the threshold, and it explains which signal changed and for how long.

When the link to Earth drops, events wait on board, in order, and are delivered after the transmission delay. Nothing is lost and nothing depends on the ground.

EVIDENCE

We did not stop at building a model. We tested whether it adds anything.

- The network has two hidden layers and 402 parameters, small enough to run on a single-board computer. We wrote it, its training loop and the simulators from scratch in TypeScript, with no machine learning library.

- We compared it with a plain statistical baseline on 300 held-out sessions per case, with the same alert rule for both.

- Usual recovery: zero false alerts in 300 sessions for both.

- Slightly slow recovery: the baseline caught 25 of 300. Our model caught 194 of 300, about 20 seconds earlier.

- Moderately slow recovery: 288 of 300 for the baseline, 300 of 300 for the model.

- 93 automated tests cover the signal simulator, quality checks, model, alert logic and link behavior.

WHY IT MATTERS

In space: crews on the Moon, in transit and on Mars need medical autonomy. Spectra is designed for the moments when no one on Earth can answer.

On Earth: the same design serves anyone far from a doctor and a reliable connection, such as remote clinics, research stations, ships and disaster response teams. Monitoring that works offline first and syncs later is useful wherever the link is weak.

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT

- Personal, not generic. Each astronaut is compared with their own pattern.

- Quality before intelligence. A loose band or a moving arm never becomes a false alarm.

- Explained events. Every alert says what changed and for how long.

- Offline first. The ground link is a destination for the record, not a requirement for the answer.

- Measured honestly. We publish the baseline comparison, including where the simple method is good enough.

FEASIBILITY

Every hardware component is commercially available today: Raspberry Pi compute board, PPG, skin-temperature and multispectral sensors, accelerometer, microcontroller with radio. The model runs in a browser, so it runs comfortably on the proposed server.

WHAT WE ARE CLEAR ABOUT

All data in the demo is synthetic. The hardware images are concept renders, not manufactured equipment. Spectra asks for a check. It does not diagnose, does not measure glucose or blood pressure, and does not recommend treatment. The multispectral channels are collected and displayed, but no health indicator is derived from them yet. Whether they help identify unreliable readings is our open research question.

WHAT COMES NEXT

Build the wristband prototype, train on measured reference sessions instead of synthetic ones, test motion and multispectral channels as model inputs, and validate the link behavior against real mission communication schedules.

TOOLS

TypeScript, Astro, Vitest, pnpm, HTML and CSS, GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions.
